Nerac
nay-RAK
n. (the Albret court town that sheltered the first French evangelicals and became Jeanne d'Albret's Reformed capital)
French Nérac, from a Gallo-Roman estate name with the suffix -acum; the chateau of the Albrets stands on the Baise in Gascony.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Nerac is the small Gascon court town that twice sheltered the French Reformation at the moment it had nowhere else to go. Marguerite of Navarre, sister of Francis I, held her court there and at Pau, and in the 1530s and 1540s she used her rank to protect the first French evangelicals when the Parlement of Paris was burning them: Jacques Lefevre d'Etaples, the translator of the French Bible, spent his last years at Nerac under her protection and died there about 1536; Gerard Roussel, Clement Marot and others of the Meaux circle found refuge; and the young Calvin is said to have visited Lefevre there. Marguerite herself never left the Roman church, and the dictionary records that her theology was a reforming Catholic mysticism rather than the Reformed faith, and that her protection was real and saved lives. Her daughter Jeanne d'Albret went further and made Nerac the Reformed capital of her sovereignty. The conference of Nerac in 1578 and 1579, between Catherine de Medici and the king of Navarre, produced the Edict of Nerac adjusting the places of surety. The dictionary enters Nerac because the French Reformation's first decade survived on the protection of a princess who did not share its doctrine.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines protection as the act of defending from evil; a court as the residence of a sovereign; refuge as shelter from danger; and mysticism as obscure religious sentiment.

expand to see more

PROTECTION, n. The act of protecting; defense; shelter from evil; preservation from loss or injury.

COURT, n. The place where a sovereign resides; the hall or chamber where justice is administered.

REFUGE, n. Shelter or protection from danger or distress; that which shelters or protects.

MYSTICISM, n. Obscurity of doctrine; the doctrine of the Mystics, who profess a pure, sublime and perfect devotion.

PRINCESS, n. A female sovereign; the daughter of a king; the consort of a prince.

Pro 31:8 — "Open thy mouth for the dumb in the cause of all such as are appointed to destruction."

Isa 1:17 — "Learn to do well; seek judgment, relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow."

Pro 24:11 — "If thou forbear to deliver them that are drawn unto death, and those that are ready to be slain;"

Modern Corruption

Gascon court town where Marguerite of Navarre sheltered Lefevre d'Etaples and the Meaux circle, and which Jeanne d'Albret made her Reformed capital.

expand to see more

The corruption to be named is the demand that a protector be sound before his protection is honoured. Marguerite of Navarre was not a Reformed believer; she stayed in the Roman church, wrote mystical verse the dictionary does not commend, and sheltered men whom the Parlement of Paris would have burned. The dictionary states both and refuses to diminish the second for the sake of the first. What she did is what Scripture commands of anyone with power: “Open thy mouth for the dumb in the cause of all such as are appointed to destruction” (Pro 31:8).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the duty of rescue laid on those in a position to perform it. “If thou forbear to deliver them that are drawn unto death” (Pro 24:11) is a warning addressed to the bystander, and the question put to Esther is the same question put to a princess at a hostile court: “who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?” (Est 4:14). Of a man who used his standing this way Job could say, “I delivered the poor that cried, and the fatherless, and him that had none to help him” (Job 29:12), and that is what Nerac was for about fifteen years.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew illem (H483), dumb, speechless; Hebrew natsal (H5337), to deliver, to snatch away; Hebrew azar (H5826), to help.

expand to see more

Hebrew illem (H483) — dumb, unable to speak; “Open thy mouth for the dumb”, Proverbs 31:8.

Hebrew chaluph (H2475) — destruction, passing away; “all such as are appointed to destruction”, Proverbs 31:8.

Hebrew natsal (H5337) — to snatch away, to deliver; “If thou forbear to deliver them that are drawn unto death”, Proverbs 24:11.

Hebrew malkuth (H4438) — royalty, a kingdom, royal estate; “thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this”, Esther 4:14.

Hebrew azar (H5826) — to help, to succour; “him that had none to help him”, Job 29:12.

Usage

"“Open thy mouth for the dumb in the cause of all such as are appointed to destruction” (Pro 31:8) — Marguerite sheltering the Meaux circle."

"“who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?” (Est 4:14) — a princess at a court that was burning men."

"“him that had none to help him” (Job 29:12) — Lefevre d'Etaples dying at Nerac about 1536."
